name: field
description:
A labelled input and everything that has to travel with it: the label, the hint, the error, and the wiring that ties them together. 30 uses, 26 of them in avenID, where the same four elements were reassembled by hand each time — which is how a field ends up with a visible error no screen reader announces.

The `shape` axis is what the claim card needed. A field with a fixed suffix — `.aven.ceo` — is not a placeholder and not a label: it is part of the control, it must not be selectable as text the user could delete, and it has to sit inside the same border so the two read as one field. That was eighty-odd utilities across two elements at the call site.

A SELECT is this unit with a different control, not a unit of its own — it was one, and the two shared their label, their shell, their focus rule and their hint. What actually differs is the tag and a marker, which is a `control` variant.

base.$description:
CONTAINER. This unit establishes an inline-size container named after itself, so anything inside it can respond to the width of THIS BOX rather than to the width of the window. That is the difference that matters for a design system: a composite dropped into a 320px sidebar and the same composite on a 320px phone are the same situation, and a viewport query calls them different ones. The library carries no viewport media query anywhere for exactly this reason — the only `@media` in it is `prefers-reduced-motion`, which is a person's setting and not a size.

`inline-size: 100%` is the container's REQUIRED companion, not a preference. `container-type: inline-size` makes the box's width independent of its contents — that is the containment being asked for — so a container with no width of its own has nothing left to size from and collapses to zero. This unit did: centred in a grid it became a column of single words. A container fills what it is given and bounds itself with `max-inline-size`; it never sizes to its text.

IT DECLARES `--icon-tint`, the colour the engine paints a duotone's secondary layer with. Declared HERE, on the unit that draws the glyph, and not once at the document root: a global custom property is the anti-pattern the whole scoping design exists to avoid — two brands on one page write the same name and the second wins. An app shell is no better, because a shell is a container that may host more than one vibe. A unit is the smallest thing that owns its own subtree, so the tint travels with the component that needs it and reaches nothing else.

control.$description: `inline-size:100%` and `min-inline-size:0` are not cosmetic. An input keeps an intrinsic width of about twenty characters, and in a grid that intrinsic width sizes the column — which is the single most common cause of a layout that overflows at 320px.

shell.$description: The border, so a suffix or an affix can sit INSIDE it. The control carries no border of its own in that shape — two borders side by side read as two fields.

suffix.$description: A fixed tail — `.aven.ceo`, a currency, a unit. `user-select:none` because it is chrome and not content: a user who drag-selects the field should get what they typed, not what the system appended.

prefix.$description: A fixed head — a scheme, a currency symbol. Same rules as suffix.

marker.$description: The chevron on a select. `pointer-events:none` or it eats the click that should open the picker.

size.$description: How big. `hero` is the single field a landing page is built around — the one the eye lands on after the headline.

shape.$description: What the control is made of. `affixed` moves the border to the shell so a prefix or suffix can live inside it; `pill` is for the one field a page is built around.

type.$description:
How the field RENDERS, which is not the same as what it accepts. `email` and `search` were options here and declared nothing at all — two switches that moved and changed no pixel, which is the same defect as a step variant that only tints a crest: it teaches the reader the control is broken.

They declared nothing because there is nothing to declare. An email field differs from a text field by `type`, `inputmode` and `autocomplete` — ATTRIBUTES on the control, which belong in the interface and are what make the right keyboard appear on a phone. A search field differs by having a leading icon and a clear button, which is composition: `shape: pill` plus a slot. Neither is a look, so neither is a styling variant.

What remains all genuinely changes how the text is set: a password's tracking, a numeric field's tabular figures, a multiline field's height and resize behaviour.

password.$description: `type=password` + `autocomplete=current-password`. Never block paste: WCAG 3.3.8 exists because blocking it forces people to retype from memory.

numeric.$description: `inputmode=numeric` rather than `type=number` — a code or a card number is a STRING of digits, and `type=number` strips leading zeros and offers a spinner nobody wants on either.

multiline.$description: A `<textarea>`. Resizes vertically only, because horizontal resize breaks the measure it was given.

control.$description: What the control IS. The label, hint, error and focus behaviour are identical across all of them, which is why they are one unit.

select.$description: A native `<select>`, deliberately: it gets the platform's own picker on a phone, works with a hardware keyboard and a screen reader without a line of JavaScript, and cannot be scrolled out of view. A custom listbox earns its cost only when the options are more than text.

focus.$description: On the SHELL, not the control — in an affixed field the input has no border of its own, so a ring on it would draw inside the shell and look like a mistake. `:focus-within` is what carries it there.

invalid.$description: The border reddens AND the ground tints, because a border alone is a 1px signal — but neither is what makes it accessible. `aria-invalid` is what a screen reader reads, and the error message says how to FIX it rather than what is wrong.

disabled.$description: No pointer events and no focus. A disabled field that still takes focus is a keyboard trap with extra steps.

a11y.note: The label is a real `<label for>`, not a placeholder — a placeholder disappears the moment someone types, taking the question with it. The error carries `role=alert` so it is announced when it appears, and is referenced by `aria-describedby` so it is read again when focus returns. `aria-invalid` is what a screen reader uses to say the field is wrong; the red border says it to everyone else, which is why both are here.
